# King's Scholar: Concise Summary
The title "King's Scholar" originates from 1317, when King Edward II established a group of 12 students at the University of Cambridge, later adopted by other prestigious schools. At Eton College, King's Scholars—also known as Collegers or "tugs"—are awarded a Foundation Scholarship following a competitive exam and reside in "College", the school's historic central house. Numbering around 70, these scholars are distinguished by wearing a black academic gown over traditional attire, reflecting their unique status and privileges such as dining in College Hall and participating in certain traditions like the Wall Game. Historically, the Foundation Scholarship covered all fees, though today it is means-tested and does not guarantee fee waivers. King's Scholars bear the "KS" post-nominal in school lists, while Oppidan Scholars (OS) are academically distinguished Oppidans who do not receive the same benefits.
The King's Scholar designation is also present in other institutions. Westminster School's foundation scholars are named King's or Queen's Scholars, depending on the monarch, selected by examination and distinguished by gowns during Abbey services. At King's College Cambridge, undergraduates receiving first-class degrees are awarded King's Scholarships, including monetary prizes and ceremonial honors. The seven King's Schools re-endowed by Henry VIII—Canterbury, Chester, Ely, Gloucester, Peterborough, Rochester, Worcester—also grant King's Scholarships for academic or musical excellence. Furthermore, King's Ely incorporates traditional privileges and ceremonies for its King's Scholars, such as the "Hoop Trundle" and lifelong connection to Ely Cathedral. Notable Eton King's Scholars include historical and contemporary figures from politics, science, literature, and the arts.
